questions.title: Classes & Objects practice 1
choices: It does not compile
It throws a NullPointerException
questions.explanation: `new` was called once, so there is exactly one object. `Student b = a;` copies the reference, not the object, so `a` and `b` are two names pointing at the same Student. Changing it through `b` changes what you see through `a`, and the answer is 2.0. If you picked 3.9, you read `b = a` as making a second student. It does not: only `new` builds an object, and there is no second `new` here.

questions.title: Classes & Objects practice 2
questions.prompt: The Student class declares `String name;` and `double gpa;` and has no constructor. What does this print?
choices: null then 0.0
It throws a NullPointerException on the first println
It does not compile, since the fields were never set
An empty line then 0
questions.explanation: `new` really did build an object, so `s` points at something and the dot works. Java fills unset fields with defaults: a `double` starts at 0.0, and any object type, including `String`, starts at `null`. So you get `null` and then `0.0`. If you picked the NullPointerException, you had the right idea about `null` but the wrong target: `s.name` is null, and `s` is not. Printing a null is fine. Only using a dot on a null crashes.

questions.title: Trace Classes & Objects
questions.prompt: What output does this code produce? Enter each line in order.
questions.explanation: The whole file. `name` and `gpa` are fields: the state each Student carries, declared once in the class and then owned separately by every object built from it. `new Student()` builds one such object and hands back a reference to it, which is what `s` holds. The resulting output is 'Ada\n3.9'.

questions.title: Classes & Objects practice 5
choices: It prints "here", then throws a NullPointerException
It prints "here", then an empty line
It prints nothing and throws immediately
It fails to compile
questions.explanation: `s` is declared but points at no object, so the first line runs and prints "here". The second line asks the object at `s` for its `name`, but there is no object, so Java throws a NullPointerException at that line. It compiles cleanly, which is what makes the bug survive to run time.

questions.title: Java class wrapper
questions.prompt: Why do small Java programs usually start inside `public class Something { ... }`?
choices: Every Java program you have written so far sat inside `public class Something { ... }`.
Store all object state in one shared global variable.
Skip constructors and fill fields only when remembered later.
Use a class when no related data or behavior is being grouped.
questions.explanation: Java organizes methods and fields inside classes. Even a first `main` program needs a class wrapper because the class is the unit Java compiles and names. That wrapper is not the same as one object, but it is the doorway into object-oriented Java.

questions.title: Using this in constructors
questions.prompt: A constructor receives `name` and the class also has a field named `name`. Why write `this.name = name`?
choices: Let outside code change every field directly.
In that constructor, the parameter is called `name` and the field is also called `name`. Java resolves the plain name `name` to the parameter, because the closer one wins.
Put unrelated responsibilities into one large class.
Forget that each object has its own instance data.
questions.explanation: `this.name` points to the field on the current object, while the plain name `name` refers to the constructor parameter nearby. Without `this`, the assignment can accidentally talk only to the parameter and leave the object field unchanged.

questions.title: Null object variable
questions.prompt: Code calls a method on an object variable that is still `null`. What is the real issue?
choices: Name methods after vague actions such as `doStuff`.
Use local variables when persistent object state is needed.
The variable does not refer to a created object yet.
Call an instance method before creating an object.
questions.explanation: `null` means the variable is not pointing at an object. The method call fails because there is no instance to receive it. The fix is to create or receive a real object before using its fields or methods.

questions.title: Class naming
questions.prompt: Which class name best communicates the thing being modeled?
choices: Treat the class blueprint as the same thing as one object.
Leave an object in a half-initialized state.
Make every method change object state even when it should only read.
Name the class for the thing it represents, capitalized: `Student`, not `doStudentStuff`.
questions.explanation: A class name should sound like the kind of thing the object represents, such as `Student` or `ParkingTicket`. Verb-like names such as `doStudentStuff` blur the difference between a type and an action.

questions.title: Fields versus methods
questions.prompt: When planning a Java class, how should a student separate fields and methods?
choices: Fields are what it knows. Methods are what it can do. Sort your ideas into those two piles first.
Use static/shared data for per-object information.
Ignore invariants that should stay true after each method call.
Mix user input directly into every object method.
questions.explanation: Fields store what each object knows, while methods describe what the object can do. Sorting ideas this way helps keep state in one place and behavior close to the data it uses.

questions.title: Constructor completeness
questions.prompt: When an object needs several required fields, why write a constructor early?
choices: Return internal mutable data without control.
Write a constructor as soon as an object needs more than one field, so an object can never exist half filled in.
Use inheritance where a helper field would be clearer.
Hide important setup in unrelated methods.
questions.explanation: A constructor lets the class require the information needed to make a valid object. That reduces half-filled instances where some later method assumes a field exists but setup was forgotten.
